Python environments

Source: vignettes/articles/python-environments.Rmd
python-environments.Rmd

xrdbi runs xarray in a Python session that R reaches through reticulate. Which Python that is, and what is installed in it, decides which data you can open. There are four ways to set it up, from least to most effort:

  1. let reticulate manage a Python for you
  2. use a Python you manage yourself
  3. use a conda (or pixi, or mamba) environment
  4. use the gdal-r-python container image

Only the GDAL engine, gdalxarray, narrows the choice: it needs the GDAL Python bindings, which pip cannot install, so it works in 3 and 4 and in 2 only when GDAL is installed there.

1. Let reticulate manage it

With no Python configured, reticulate builds one with uv, from the requirements packages declare with reticulate::py_require(). Loading xrdbi declares the core:

  • xarray, which brings pandas and numpy
  • netCDF4, the engine for local netCDF-3 and netCDF-4 files

That is all the Get started vignette needs. Every other source needs its engine, declared the same way, ideally before the first connection:

library(xrdbi)
reticulate::py_require("zarr")                   # zarr stores
reticulate::py_require(c("zarr", "gcsfs"))       # zarr on Google Cloud
reticulate::py_require(c("zarr", "s3fs"))        # zarr on S3
reticulate::py_require(c("h5netcdf", "h5py", "fsspec", "aiohttp"))
                                                 # netCDF/HDF5 over HTTPS
reticulate::py_require("dask")                   # open_mfdataset
reticulate::py_require(c("xvec", "geopandas"))   # vector data cubes

If Python has already started, reticulate switches to an environment that adds them. uv caches what it downloads, so later sessions start quickly.

This is the easy path, and it covers zarr, netCDF and HDF5, local or remote. It cannot give you gdalxarray: GDAL’s Python bindings come from a GDAL installation, not from PyPI.

2. A Python you manage yourself

Point reticulate at an interpreter with RETICULATE_PYTHON, in ~/.Renviron or before reticulate starts:

Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = "/path/to/venv/bin/python")
library(xrdbi)

A virtual environment that is activated in the shell (VIRTUAL_ENV is set) is found without it. Either way, reticulate uses that Python as it is: it does not install into it, even what py_require() declares. Install the packages yourself:

/path/to/venv/bin/python -m pip install xarray netCDF4 zarr h5netcdf

gdalxarray works here if this Python has the GDAL bindings (from osgeo import gdal succeeds), as a system Python with GDAL from your distribution often does.

3. conda, pixi or mamba

conda-forge has GDAL and its Python bindings, so a conda environment can hold everything, gdalxarray included:

conda create -n xr -c conda-forge python xarray netcdf4 zarr gcsfs \
  h5netcdf gdal gdalxarray libpython micromamba
conda activate xr

Three things need care, each found by testing:

  • reticulate does not look at the activated environment. It honours VIRTUAL_ENV, not CONDA_PREFIX, and with requirements declared it builds its own environment from PyPI instead. Set the interpreter explicitly:

    export RETICULATE_PYTHON="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python"

  • reticulate needs the shared libpython, which conda-forge ships as its own package, libpython. Without it, reticulate stops with “Python shared library not found”.

  • reticulate wants a conda binary. For a Python in a conda-layout environment, it runs conda run once to learn the environment’s PATH, and fails with “Unable to find conda binary” if no conda, mamba or micromamba is on PATH or in the usual places. That is the case in pixi environments, hence micromamba in the environment above.

The draft conda-forge recipe in tools/conda handles all three: its activation script sets RETICULATE_PYTHON, and it depends on libpython and micromamba.

4. The gdal-r-python image

ghcr.io/hypertidy/gdal-r-python is a container image with R, GDAL, the GDAL Python bindings and a Python geospatial stack, including xarray, zarr, netCDF4, h5netcdf, dask, rasterix and gdalxarray. RETICULATE_PYTHON is set to its Python, so reticulate uses it as is. This site is built in it.

docker run --rm -it ghcr.io/hypertidy/gdal-r-python:latest R
pak::pak("mdsumner/xrdbi")

Add Python packages with uv, into the image’s Python. The README’s ERA5 example needs gcsfs, and vector cubes need xvec:

uv pip install --python "$RETICULATE_PYTHON" gcsfs xvec

The image runs development dask with its array query planning turned on, under which xarray’s open_mfdataset() fails with a NotImplementedError. Turn it off for the container, as this site’s build does:

docker run --rm -it -e DASK_ARRAY__QUERY_PLANNING=False ghcr.io/hypertidy/gdal-r-python:latest R

Check what you have

reticulate::py_config() says which Python was chosen and why, and xarray lists the engines it can use:

reticulate::py_config()
reticulate::import("xarray")$backends$list_engines()
reticulate::py_module_available("gdalxarray")

An engine that is not installed fails at dbConnect(), with xarray’s message naming it and listing the engines it has (“unrecognized engine ‘zarr’ must be one of your download engines: …”). Declare it with py_require() (setup 1) or install it into your Python (2, 3 and 4).

Credentials and network settings

Remote data is read by Python, so Python’s settings apply:

  • fsspec-based engines (zarr on gcsfs or s3fs, h5netcdf over HTTPS) take storage_options, passed through dbConnect(), for example storage_options = reticulate::dict(token = "anon") for a public Google Cloud bucket.
  • GDAL reads its configuration from the process environment when it accesses data, so Sys.setenv(AWS_NO_SIGN_REQUEST = "YES") from R works for public S3 buckets read through gdalxarray.
